3.evidence_source: “This study examined the psychometric properties of the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2) in Brazilian adolescents.”
3._section_summary: This section reports one validation study (Study X) of the BAS-2 in Brazilian adolescents (N = 840; 438 boys, 402 girls; mean ages ≈15.5). Confirmatory factor analysis supported a unidimensional and partially invariant factor structure across gender and weight status; the BAS-2 showed adequate internal consistency and two-week temporal stability, and body appreciation was negatively associated with BMI in both boys and girls.

4.evidence_source: As a contribution to the body image literature, the aim of this study was to examine the psychometric properties of the BAS-2 in Brazilian adolescents.
4._section_summary: This Introduction describes the development and validation history of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) and its revision (BAS-2), and states that the present study aims to examine the psychometric properties of the BAS-2 in Brazilian adolescents. The authors hypothesize a one-factor structure invariant across gender and weight status, good internal consistency and two-week temporal stability, and expected correlations of BAS-2 with life satisfaction (positive) and with social physique anxiety and BMI (negative).

5.evidence_source: The sample was comprised of 840 students (438 boys and 402 girls) from three Brazilian cities located in São Paulo State.
5._section_summary: This section describes a sample of 840 students (438 boys, 402 girls) from three Brazilian cities in São Paulo State aged 13–17, with gender-specific mean ages (boys 15.50, girls 15.51) and mean BMIs (boys 21.87, girls 21.67). It also reports a second independent test-retest sample of 46 students (19 boys, 27 girls; Mage = 14.02, MBMI = 20.32) who completed the BAS-2 twice within two weeks to assess temporal stability.

6.evidence_source: Participants completed a Brazilian Portuguese translation (see Table 1) of the BAS-2 (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Additionally, the SWLS is described as 'validated in Brazilian adolescent population' and Brazilian adolescent BMI cut-offs (Conde & Monteiro, 2006) were used.
6._section_summary: This section lists measures used in a single study of Brazilian adolescents: a Brazilian Portuguese BAS-2 for body appreciation, a Portuguese adolescent Social Physique Anxiety Scale, and the Portuguese SWLS validated for Brazilian adolescents. Demographics collected included gender, age, height, and weight; BMI was computed from self-reported height and weight and classified using Brazilian adolescent cut-offs. No sample size, survey administration method, racial composition, mean age, mean BMI, or correlations between body appreciation and BMI are reported in the provided text.

7._section_summary: The section reports a confirmatory factor analysis of a hypothesized 10-item one-factor BAS-2 model showing acceptable fit for the whole sample and for gender and weight-status subsamples. DIFFTEST indicated a statistically significant difference between M0 and M1 across gender (p = .01), and freeing two item thresholds (M1P) removed that significance (M1P vs. M0, p = .07); invariance across weight status showed no significant difference (M1 vs. M0, p = .33). The table lists subgroup sample sizes (Boys n = 438; Girls n = 402; Underweight & Normoweight n = 592; Overweight & Obese n = 248). No explicit labels such as 'Study 1' or 'Experiment 2' are used.

8.evidence_source: This study examined the psychometric properties of a Brazilian Portuguese translation of the  BAS-2 in Brazilian adolescents.
8._section_summary: This Discussion summarizes a single study that evaluated the Brazilian Portuguese translation of the BAS-2 in Brazilian adolescents, reporting a one-dimensional factor structure, gender invariance, adequate reliability, and convergent/incremental validity. It notes a negative relationship between body appreciation and BMI (reported qualitatively), uses a convenience sample from three Brazilian cities, and highlights limitations including the non-representative sample and cross-sectional design.
